name: Killybegs
title: Killybegs Fishing Vessel Thickness Measurement | UTM
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Killybegs, Ireland's main fishing port: pelagic trawlers, RSW tanks, hull structure, shiplift preparation and piping.
h1: Hull Gauging for Fishing Vessels and Workboats at Killybegs
intro: Killybegs, on the south coast of Donegal, is Ireland's principal fishing port and a designated fishery harbour centre, home to the pelagic trawler fleet and a busy mix of processing, repair and service activity. Fishing vessels work hard in a corrosive setting, and owners, insurers and buyers want measured steel before dockings and sales. A team mobilised from India gauges vessels alongside the quays, on the shiplift apron or during winter lay-up.

highlights.p: Large pelagic freezer and refrigerated seawater trawlers spend long seasons at sea. Their tanks, side shell and decks wear in ways that readings can quantify before a docking, a sale or an insurer's request.

Vessels lifted out for repair benefit from gauging done beforehand, since the yard can scope steel renewal and plan the slot before the lift. After the lift, bottom and shell plating are open for a final check.

Pelagic fishing runs in seasons set by quota, and boats return to port for fuel, gear and repair. Winter lay-up and the breaks between fisheries are the windows when a team can work without disturbing the fishing.

port.h: Killybegs: a deep, sheltered fishery harbour in Donegal Bay
p: Killybegs lies on the northern shore of Donegal Bay, in a natural inlet that gives deep water close to the town and good shelter from the Atlantic. The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine runs it as one of Ireland's fishery harbour centres, and the harbour is arranged around the working fleet: long quays for landing, ice, fuel and gear, processing plants along the waterfront, and boatyards and engineering shops that keep the boats going. Pilotage exemption certificates are common among regular masters, and the approach is straightforward in most weather.

The fleet is the heart of the port. Large pelagic trawlers fish for mackerel, herring, blue whiting and horse mackerel, and landings feed local processing factories and the export trade. Alongside them come whitefish trawlers, smaller netters and potters, aquaculture service boats and, at times, vessels from other EU fleets that land or take on supplies. The harbour also receives general cargo, fish meal and fish oil carriers, occasional cruise calls, naval and fishery protection vessels, and offshore project cargo, so a steel survey here can mean a trawler one week and a cargo coaster the next.

Seasonal patterns decide when vessels are available. Pelagic fisheries have defined seasons, and when the quota is caught or the season closes, boats come back to port and queue for repair slots. Weather is the other constraint: winter gales can keep boats alongside for days, which in practice makes them available for gauging. Summer is the busiest period for fishing and for cruise visitors, so a team planning a job often prefers the shoulder months, when quays are less congested and yards less booked.

facilities.h: Where fishing vessels and workboats can be gauged at Killybegs
p: Killybegs has a shiplift and repair yards that handle fishing vessels, and this is the reason many owners choose to carry out maintenance here. Gauging is best planned in two stages. Before the lift, tanks and accessible structure are measured so that the yard can fix the steel scope and book the slot. Once the vessel is out of the water, the bottom, bilge keels, rudder and the shell around the waterline are open to final readings, and any renewal can be checked as it is fitted.

Away from the lift, a vessel alongside a landing quay is available between discharge and sailing. Refrigerated seawater tanks, fish holds, fuel and ballast tanks and the deck structure around winches and gantries can be gauged once the spaces are clean and certified safe. Fishing vessels often have heavily modified superstructure and tank arrangements, so we gauge to the owner's drawings where they exist and record the layout found on board where they do not.
list: Killybegs shiplift and repair yards — pre-lift tank gauging and post-lift shell and bottom plating readings on fishing vessels and workboats.
Main landing quays — RSW tank, fish hold and deck gauging on pelagic trawlers between discharge and sailing.
Lay-up berths — longer condition gauging on trawlers idle between fishing seasons or awaiting sale.
Deep-water quay — hull and piping gauging on cargo ships, fish-meal carriers and visiting cruise or naval vessels.
Harbour anchorage — launch-assisted gauging of cleaned tanks on vessels waiting for a berth in calm conditions.

context.h: Fishing vessel rules and Irish port state control at Killybegs
p: Fishing vessels fall under a different rule set from cargo ships. In Ireland, the Marine Survey Office of the Department of Transport certifies and surveys the national fleet, and many boats are not classed, so a gauging report may be used by the owner, the insurer or the buyer rather than a class surveyor. Larger pelagic trawlers and some other vessels do follow a class society's rules, and for those the reading format and extent follow the society's requirements. Foreign cargo ships calling at Killybegs are subject to Paris MoU port state control in the usual way.

Steel condition matters commercially as well as legally. Buyers of second-hand trawlers, banks financing vessel purchases and insurers renewing hull cover all ask for evidence of the plating's condition, and a thickness report is a straightforward way to give it. EU rules on ship recycling and the Inventory of Hazardous Materials apply to ships of the relevant size, and the owner of an ageing boat deciding between a major refit and replacement needs the measured wastage to make that call sensibly.

jobs.p: Most jobs here are driven by the fishing calendar and the yard schedule. A scope is agreed with the skipper or technical manager, set against the vessel's drawings, and timed to a break in fishing. We carry the equipment into confined spaces only after the crew confirm they are clean and safe, and the report is laid out by tank or area so the yard, the insurer or the buyer can read it without translation.
list: Pre-lift gauging of a pelagic trawler's RSW tanks, fuel tanks and accessible side shell, ahead of a repair slot at the shiplift.
Post-lift readings on bottom plating, rudder and bilge keels, taken once the vessel is on the lift.
Pre-purchase condition gauging on a second-hand trawler for a buyer or a bank.
Deck plating and winch foundation gauging on a whitefish trawler returning from a long season.
Piping and hull checks on a fish-meal carrier or general cargo ship alongside the deep-water quay.

logistics: Donegal Airport at Carrickfinn has limited services, so most travellers fly into Dublin or Knock and continue by road, or arrive through Belfast or Derry and cross the border. Technicians travel from India on Irish visas, with extra visa planning if the route passes through the UK. Quay access and any work near the processing plants is arranged through the vessel's agent or the owner's representative, and plans leave room for gales and fishing schedule changes.

faqs.q: Can you gauge a fishing vessel's refrigerated seawater tanks?
faqs.a: Yes, once the tanks are drained, cleaned and ventilated, and the crew have issued the entry permit. RSW tanks suffer corrosion at welds, stiffeners and the tank top, so we measure those details first and report by tank. If the vessel will be lifted, gauging beforehand lets the yard plan the steel renewal.

faqs.q: Do unclassed fishing vessels need thickness measurement?
faqs.a: There may be no class rule requiring it, but owners, insurers and buyers often ask for it. A report gives measured plate thickness against the original and shows where wastage is concentrated. It is useful when buying a boat, renewing insurance or deciding whether to repair or replace, and it can be presented to the Marine Survey Office if asked.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock at Killybegs?
faqs.a: Killybegs has a shiplift and repair yards that handle fishing vessels and smaller ships, not a conventional graving dock of the kind used by large merchant ships. Larger ships needing a full docking go to a yard in another port. We gauge before the lift to inform the steel scope and again once the vessel is out of the water.

faqs.q: When is the best time to gauge a pelagic trawler at Killybegs?
faqs.a: Between fisheries, when the boat is alongside for repairs or waiting for the next season, and in winter weather that keeps the fleet in port. We plan around the owner's quota calendar and yard slots, and aim to finish tank work early enough that any renewals can be scheduled before the vessel sails again.
